stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 1
summaryBullets: It was after this that the following things happened in the days of Artaxerxes, the same Artaxerxes who ruled over one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. (1:1).
In those days, when King Artaxerxes was enthroned in the city of Susa, (1:2).
in the third year of his reign, he gave a banquet for his Friends and other persons of various nations, the Persians and Median nobles, and the governors of the satrapies. (1:3).
After this, when he had displayed to them the riches of his kingdom and the splendor of his bountiful celebration during the course of one hundred eighty days, (1:4).
at the end of the wedding feast the king gave a drinking party for the people of various nations who lived in the city. This was held for six days in the courtyard of the royal palace, (1:5).

which was adorned with curtains of fine linen and cotton, held by cords of linen and purple fabric attached to gold and silver blocks on pillars of marble and other stones. Gold and silver couches were placed on a mosaic floor of emerald, mother-of-pearl, and marble. There were coverings of gauze, embroidered in various colors, with roses scattered around them. (1:6).
The cups were of gold and silver, and a miniature cup was displayed, made of ruby, worth thirty thousand talents. There was abundant sweet wine, such as the king himself drank. (1:7).
This drinking party was not in accordance with established custom, but the king wished to have it so, and he commanded his stewards to comply with his pleasure and with that of the guests. (1:8).
Meanwhile, Queen Vashti gave a drinking party for the women in the palace where King Artaxerxes was. (1:9).
On the seventh day, when the king was in good humor, he told Haman, Bazan, Tharra, Boraze, Zatholtha, Abataza, and Tharaba, the seven eunuchs who served King Artaxerxes, (1:10).

to escort the queen to him in order to proclaim her as queen and to place the diadem on her head and to have her display her beauty to all the governors and the people of various nations, for she was indeed a beautiful woman. (1:11).
But Queen Vashti refused to obey him and would not come with the eunuchs. This offended the king, and he became furious. (1:12).
He said to his Friends, “This is how Vashti has answered me. Give, therefore, your ruling and judgment on this matter.” (1:13).
Arkesaeus, Sarsathaeus, and Malesear, the governors of the Persians and Medes who were closest to the king, who sat beside him in the chief seats, came to him (1:14).
and told him what, according to the law, was to be done to Queen Vashti for not obeying the order that the king had sent her by the eunuchs. (1:15).
Then Muchaeus said to the king and the governors, “Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king but also all the king’s governors and officials” (1:16).
(for he had reported to them what the queen had said and how she had defied the king). “And just as she defied King Artaxerxes, (1:17).
so now the other noble wives of the Persian and Median governors, on hearing what she has said to the king, will likewise dare to dishonor their husbands. (1:18).

If, therefore, it pleases the king, let him issue a royal decree, inscribed in accordance with the laws of the Medes and Persians so that it may not be altered, that the queen may no longer come into his presence, and let the king give her royal rank to a woman better than she. (1:19).
Let whatever law the king enacts be proclaimed in his kingdom, and thus all women will give honor to their husbands, rich and poor alike.” (1:20).
This speech pleased the king and the governors, and the king did as Muchaeus had recommended. (1:21).
The king sent the decree into all his kingdom, to every province in its own language, so that men would be feared in their households. (1:22).
crossRefs: Genesis 41:1–32 — Dreams as divine foreshadowing.
Daniel 2:28 — God reveals mysteries.
Esther 6:1–3 — Mordecai’s loyalty remembered later.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּנִּין (tannîn, 'dragon/serpent') — Greek: δράκοντες (drákontes) — Aramaic: תניניא (tannīnyā)
translationNotes.note: Symbolic figures representing opposing forces in Mordecai’s vision, later understood as Haman and Mordecai.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai’s dream foreshadows Israel’s coming danger and deliverance, and his loyalty to the king is established.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 2
summaryBullets: After these things, the king’s anger abated, and he no longer remembered Vashti or remembered what he had said and how he had condemned her. (2:1).
Then the king’s servants said, “Let beautiful and virtuous young women be sought out for the king. (2:2).

The king shall appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, and they shall select beautiful young virgins to be brought to the harem in the city of Susa. Let them be entrusted to the king’s eunuch who is in charge of the women, and let ointments and whatever else they need be given them. (2:3).
And the woman who pleases the king shall be queen instead of Vashti.” This pleased the king, and he did so. (2:4).
Now there was a Jew in the city of Susa whose name was Mordecai son of Jair son of Shimei son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin; (2:5).
he had been taken captive from Jerusalem among those whom King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had captured. (2:6).

And he had a foster child, the daughter of his father’s brother, Aminadab, and her name was Esther. When her parents died, he brought her up as a wife for himself. The young woman was beautiful in appearance. (2:7).
So when the decree of the king was proclaimed and many young women were gathered in the city of Susa in custody of Gai, Esther also was brought to Gai, who had custody of the women. (2:8).

The young woman pleased him and won his favor, and he quickly provided her with ointments and her portion of food, as well as seven young women chosen from the palace; he treated her and her maids with special favor in the harem. (2:9).
Now Esther had not disclosed her people or country, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known. (2:10).
And every day Mordecai walked in the courtyard of the harem, to see what would happen to Esther. (2:11).

Now the period after which a young woman was to go to the king was twelve months. During this time the days of cosmetic treatment are completed: six months while they are anointing themselves with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments for women. (2:12).
Then she goes in to the king; she is handed to the person appointed and goes with him from the harem to the king’s palace. (2:13).

In the evening she enters, and in the morning she departs to the second harem, where Gai the king’s eunuch is in charge of the women, and she does not go in to the king again unless she is summoned by name. (2:14).

When the time was fulfilled for Esther daughter of Aminadab, the brother of Mordecai’s father, to go in to the king, she neglected none of the things that the eunuch in charge of the women had commanded. For Esther found favor in the eyes of all who saw her. (2:15).
So Esther went in to King Artaxerxes in the twelfth month, which is Adar, in the seventh year of his reign. (2:16).
And the king loved Esther passionately, and she found favor beyond all the other virgins, and he put on her the queen’s diadem. (2:17).

Then the king gave a drinking party lasting seven days for all his Friends and the officers to celebrate his marriage to Esther, and he granted a remission of taxes to those who were under his rule. (2:18).
Meanwhile Mordecai was serving in the court. (2:19).
Esther had not disclosed her country, for thus Mordecai had instructed her to fear God and keep his laws, just as she had done when she was with him. So Esther did not change her way of life. (2:20).
Now two of the king’s eunuchs, who were chief bodyguards, were upset because of Mordecai’s advancement, and they plotted to kill King Artaxerxes. (2:21).
The matter became known to Mordecai, and he warned Esther, who in turn revealed the plot to the king. (2:22).
He investigated the two eunuchs and hanged them. Then the king ordered that a record commemorating Mordecai’s goodwill be deposited in the royal archive. (2:23).
crossRefs: Genesis 41:1–32 — Dreams as divine foreshadowing.
Daniel 2:28 — God reveals mysteries.
Esther 6:1–3 — Mordecai’s loyalty remembered later.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 3
summaryBullets: This is a copy of the letter: “The Great King, Artaxerxes, writes the following to the governors of the hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia and to the officials under them: (3:1).

“Having become ruler of many nations and master of the whole world (not elated with presumption of authority but always acting reasonably and with kindness), I have determined to settle the lives of my subjects in lasting tranquility and, in order to make my kingdom peaceable and open to travel throughout all its extent, to restore the peace desired by all people. (3:2).

“When I asked my counselors how this might be accomplished, Haman—who excels among us in sound judgment and is distinguished for his unchanging goodwill and steadfast fidelity and has attained the second place of honor in the kingdom — (3:3).

pointed out to us that among all the nations in the world there is scattered a certain hostile people who have laws contrary to those of every nation and continually disregard the ordinances of kings, so that the unifying of the kingdom that we honorably intend cannot be brought about. (3:4).

We understand that this people, and it alone, stands constantly in opposition to all humanity, perversely following a strange manner of life and laws, and is ill-disposed to our interests, doing all the harm they can so that our kingdom may not attain stability. (3:5).

“Therefore we have decreed that those indicated to you in the letters written by Haman, who is in charge of affairs and is our second father, shall all—wives and children included—be utterly destroyed by the swords of their enemies, without pity or restraint, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, of this present year, (3:6).
so that those who have long been hostile and remain so may in a single day go down in violence to Hades and leave our interests secure and untroubled hereafter.” (3:7).

Then Haman said to King Artaxerxes, “There is a certain nation scattered among the other nations in all your kingdom; their laws are different from those of every other nation, and they do not keep the laws of the king. It is not expedient for the king to tolerate them. (3:8).
If it pleases the king, let him decree that they are to be destroyed, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into the king’s treasury.” (3:9).
So the king took off his signet ring and gave it to Haman to seal the decree that was to be written against the Jews. (3:10).
The king told Haman, “Keep the money, and do whatever you want with that nation.” (3:11).

So on the thirteenth day of the first month the king’s secretaries were summoned, and in accordance with Haman’s instructions they wrote in the name of King Artaxerxes to the magistrates and the governors in every province from India to Ethiopia, one hundred twenty-seven provinces in all, and to the governors of the nations, each in his own language. (3:12).
Instructions were sent by couriers throughout all the empire of Artaxerxes to destroy the Jewish people in a single day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, and to plunder their goods. (3:13).
Copies of the letter were posted in every province, and all the nations were ordered to be prepared for that day. (3:14).
The matter was expedited also in Susa. And while the king and Haman caroused together, the city was thrown into confusion. (3:15).
crossRefs: Ezra 9:6–15 — Confession of national sin.
Daniel 9:4–19 — Prayer of intercession in exile.
Hebrews 4:16 — Approach God’s throne with boldness.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק וָאֵפֶר (śaq wāʾefer) — Greek: σάκκος καὶ σποδός (sákkos kai spodós) — Aramaic: שק ואפר (saq wʾapr)
translationNotes.note: Traditional signs of mourning and repentance used throughout the Hebrew Scriptures.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai and Esther pray earnestly for God’s help as the decree of destruction threatens Israel.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 4
summaryBullets: When Mordecai learned of all that had been done, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and sprinkled himself with ashes; then he rushed through the street of the city, shouting loudly: “An innocent nation is being destroyed!” (4:1).
He got as far as the king’s gate, and there he stopped, because no one was allowed to enter the courtyard clothed in sackcloth and ashes. (4:2).
And in every province where the letter had been posted there was crying, lamentation, and great mourning among the Jews, and they put on sackcloth and ashes. (4:3).

When the queen’s maids and eunuchs came and told her, she was deeply troubled by what she heard had happened and sent instructions to clothe Mordecai and to remove his sackcloth, but he would not consent. (4:4).
Then Esther summoned Hachratheus, the eunuch who attended her, and dispatched him to get accurate information for her from Mordecai. (4:5).
So Mordecai told him what had happened and about the promise that Haman had promised the king: ten thousand talents for the royal treasury to bring about the destruction of the Jews. (4:7).

He also gave him a copy of what had been posted in Susa for their destruction, to show to Esther, and he told him to charge her to go in to the king and plead for his favor in behalf of the people. “Remember,” he said, “the days when you were an ordinary person, being brought up under my care, for Haman, who is second to the king, has spoken against us and demands our death. Call upon the Lord; then speak to the king in our behalf and save us from death.” (4:8).
Hachratheus went in and told her all these things. (4:9).
And Esther said to him, “Go to Mordecai and say: (4:10).

All nations of the realm know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is no escape for that person. Only the one to whom the king stretches out the golden scepter is safe—and it is now thirty days since I myself was called to go to the king.” (4:11).
So Hachratheus delivered Esther’s entire message to Mordecai, (4:12).
and then Mordecai said to Hachratheus, “Go and say to her: Esther, do not say to yourself that you alone among all the Jews in the realm will escape alive. (4:13).

For if you take no heed at such a time as this, help and protection will come to the Jews from another quarter, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows whether it was not for such a time as this that you were made queen?” (4:14).
Then Esther gave the messenger this answer to take back to Mordecai: (4:15).

“Go and gather the Jews who are in Susa and fast on my behalf; for three days and nights do not eat or drink, and my maids and I will also go without food. After that I will go to the king, contrary to the law, even if I must die.” (4:16).
So Mordecai went away and did what Esther had told him to do. (4:17).
crossRefs: Ezra 9:6–15 — Confession of national sin.
Daniel 9:4–19 — Prayer of intercession in exile.
Hebrews 4:16 — Approach God’s throne with boldness.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 5
summaryBullets: On the third day, when she ended her prayer, she took off the garments in which she had worshiped and arrayed herself in the garments of her honor. (5:1).
Then, majestically adorned, after invoking the aid of the all-seeing God and Savior, she took two maids with her; (5:2).
The king said to her, “What do you wish, Esther? What is your request? It shall be yours, even to half of my kingdom.” (5:3).
And Esther said, “Today is a special day for me. If it pleases the king, let him and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare today.” (5:4).
Then the king said, “Bring Haman quickly, so that we may do as Esther desires.” So they both came to the banquet that Esther had spoken about. (5:5).
While they were drinking wine, the king said to Esther, “What is it, Queen Esther? It shall be granted you.” (5:6).
She said, “My petition and request is: (5:7).
if I have found favor in the sight of the king, let the king and Haman come again tomorrow to the banquet that I shall prepare them, and tomorrow I will do the same.” (5:8).
So Haman went out from the king joyful and glad of heart. But when he saw Mordecai the Jew in the courtyard, he was filled with anger. (5:9).
Nevertheless, he went home and summoned his friends and his wife Zosara. (5:10).
And he told them about his riches and the honor that the king had bestowed on him and how he had advanced him to be the first in the kingdom. (5:11).
And Haman said, “The queen did not invite anyone to the banquet with the king except me, and I am invited again tomorrow. (5:12).
But these things give me no pleasure as long as I see Mordecai the Jew in the courtyard.” (5:13).

His wife Zosara and his friends said to him, “Let a pole be cut, fifty cubits high, and in the morning tell the king and have Mordecai hung on it. Then, go with the king to the banquet and enjoy yourself.” This advice pleased Haman, so the pole was prepared. (5:14).
And while she was speaking, she fainted and fell. (5:15).
Then the king was agitated, and all his attendants tried to comfort her. (5:16).
And your servant has not eaten at Haman’s table, and I have not honored the king’s feast or drunk the wine of libations. (5:17).
Your servant has had no joy since the day that I was brought here until now, except in you, O Lord God of Abraham. (5:18).
O God, whose might is over all, hear the voice of the despairing and save us from the hands of evildoers. And save me from my fear!” (5:19).
crossRefs: Genesis 32:11 — Jacob fears but prays for deliverance.
Nehemiah 2:1–5 — Cupbearer’s fear before the king.
Proverbs 21:1 — King’s heart in God’s hand.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁרְבִיט זָהָב (šarbîṭ zahāb) — Greek: σκῆπτρον χρυσοῦν (skēptron chrysoûn) — Aramaic: שרביטא דדהבא (šarbīṭā d’dahabā)
translationNotes.note: Symbol of royal authority; Esther’s life depended on the king’s gesture of acceptance.

stories.keyTakeaway: Esther risks her life before the king, but God grants her favor as Haman’s plot continues.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 6
summaryBullets: That night the Lord took sleep from the king, so he told his teacher to bring the book of daily records and to read to him. (6:1).
He found the words written about Mordecai, how he had told the king about the two royal eunuchs who were on guard and sought to lay hands on Artaxerxes. (6:2).
The king said, “What honor or favor did we bestow on Mordecai?” The king’s servants said, “You have not done anything for him.” (6:3).

While the king was inquiring about the goodwill shown by Mordecai—Look! Haman was in the courtyard. The king asked, “Who is in the courtyard?” Now Haman had come to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the pole that he had prepared. (6:4).
The servants of the king said, “Look! Haman is standing in the courtyard.” And the king said, “Summon him.” (6:5).
Then the king said to Haman, “What shall I do for the person whom I wish to honor?” And Haman said to himself, “Whom would the king wish to honor more than me?” (6:6).
So he said to the king, “For a person whom the king wishes to honor, (6:7).
let the king’s servants bring out the fine linen robe that the king wears and the horse on which the king rides, (6:8).

and let them be given to one of the king’s honored Friends, and let him robe the person whom the king loves and mount him on the horse, and let him proclaim through the open square of the city, saying, ‘Thus shall it be done to everyone whom the king honors.’ ” (6:9).
Then the king said to Haman, “You have spoken well! Do just as you have said for Mordecai the Jew who serves at court. And let not a word of what you have said be omitted.” (6:10).

So Haman got the robe and the horse; he put the robe on Mordecai, mounted him on the horse, and went through the open square of the city, proclaiming, “Thus shall it be done to everyone whom the king wishes to honor.” (6:11).
Then Mordecai returned to the courtyard, but Haman returned home, mourning and with his head covered. (6:12).

Haman told his wife Zosara and his friends what had befallen him. His friends and his wife said to him, “If Mordecai is of the Jewish people and you have begun to be humiliated before him, you will surely fall. You will not be able to defend yourself, because a living god is with him.” (6:13).
While they were still talking, the eunuchs arrived and hurriedly brought Haman to the drinking party that Esther had prepared. (6:14).

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 7
summaryBullets: So the king and Haman went in to drink with the queen. (7:1).

And the second day, as they were drinking wine, the king said, “What is it, Queen Esther? What is your petition, and what is your request? It shall be granted to you, even to half of my kingdom.” (7:2).
She answered and said, “If I have found favor with the king, let my life be granted me at my petition and my people at my request. (7:3).

For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, plundered, and made slaves—we and our children—male and female slaves. I took no heed, but now our adversary brings shame on the king’s court.” (7:4).
Then the king said, “Who is the person who would dare to do this thing?” (7:5).
Esther said, “Our enemy is this evil man Haman!” At this, Haman was terrified in the presence of the king and queen. (7:6).
The king rose from the banquet and went into the garden, and Haman began to beg for his life from the queen, for he saw that he was in serious trouble. (7:7).

When the king returned from the garden, Haman had thrown himself on the couch, pleading with the queen. The king said, “Will you dare even assault my wife in my own house?” Haman, when he heard, turned away his face. (7:8).

Then Bugathan, one of the eunuchs, said to the king, “Look, Haman has even prepared a pole for Mordecai, who gave information of concern to the king; it is standing at Haman’s house, a pole fifty cubits high.” So the king said, “Let Haman be executed on that.” (7:9).
So Haman was hung on the pole that had been prepared for Mordecai. With that the anger of the king abated. (7:10).

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 8
summaryBullets: The following is a copy of this letter: “The Great King, Artaxerxes, to the governors of the provinces from India to Ethiopia, one hundred twenty-seven provinces, and to those who are loyal to our government, greetings. (8:1).
“Many people, the more they are honored with the most generous kindness of their benefactors, the more proud do they become, (8:2).
and not only seek to injure our subjects, but in their inability to stand prosperity, they even undertake to scheme against their own benefactors. (8:3).

They not only take away thankfulness from others, but, carried away by the boasts of those who know nothing of goodness, they even assume that they will escape the evil-hating justice of God, who always sees everything. (8:4).

And often many of those who are set in places of authority have been made in part responsible for the shedding of innocent blood and have been involved in irremediable calamities, by the persuasion of friends who have been entrusted with the administration of public affairs, (8:5).
when these persons by the false trickery of their evil natures beguile the sincere goodwill of their sovereigns. (8:6).

“What has been wickedly accomplished through the pestilent behavior of those who exercise authority unworthily can be seen not so much from the more ancient records that we hand on as from investigation of matters close at hand. (8:7).
In the future we will take care to render our kingdom quiet and peaceable for all, (8:8).
by changing our methods and always judging what comes before our eyes with more equitable consideration. (8:9).
For Haman son of Hammedatha, a Macedonian (really an alien to the Persian blood and quite devoid of our kindliness), having become our guest, (8:10).
enjoyed so fully the goodwill that we have for every nation that he was called our father and was continually bowed down to by all as the person second to the royal throne. (8:11).
But, unable to restrain his arrogance, he undertook to deprive us of our kingdom and our life (8:12).
“Let copies of the decree be posted conspicuously in all the kingdom, and let all the Jews be ready on that day to fight against their enemies.” (8:13).
So the messengers on horseback set out with all speed to perform what the king had commanded, and the decree was posted also in Susa. (8:14).
Mordecai went out dressed in the royal robe and wearing a gold crown and a turban of purple linen. The people in Susa rejoiced on seeing him. (8:15).
And the Jews had light and gladness (8:16).

in every city and province wherever the decree was published; wherever the proclamation was made, the Jews had joy and gladness, a banquet and a holiday. And many of the nations were circumcised and became Jews out of fear of the Jews. (8:17).

since he, the one who did these things, has been executed at the gates of Susa with all his household—for God, who rules over all things, has speedily inflicted on him the punishment that he deserved. (8:18).
“Therefore post a copy of this letter publicly in every place and permit the Jews to live according to their own customs. (8:19).
And lend them support, so that on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, on that very day, they may defend themselves against those who attack them at the time of affliction. (8:20).
For God, who rules over all things, has made this day to be a joy for his chosen people instead of a day of destruction for them. (8:21).
“Therefore you shall observe this with all good cheer as a notable day among your commemorative festivals, (8:22).
so that both now and hereafter it may represent deliverance for us and for those loyal to the Persians but a reminder of destruction for those who plot against us. (8:23).

“Every city and country, without exception, that does not act accordingly shall be destroyed in wrath with spear and fire. It shall be made not only impassable for humans but also most hateful to wild animals and birds for all time. (8:24).
crossRefs: Exodus 17:9–14 — Israel defends against Amalek.
Isaiah 54:17 — No weapon formed shall prosper.
Romans 8:31 — If God is for us, who can be against us?

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גְּזֵרָה (gəzērāh, 'decree') — Greek: διάταγμα (diátagma) — Aramaic: גזרתא (gəzerātā)
translationNotes.note: An official royal decree, written and sealed, considered irrevocable in Persian law.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai’s counter-edict reverses Haman’s plot, bringing relief and honor to the Jews.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 9
summaryBullets: Now on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, the letter written by the king arrived. (9:1).
On that same day the enemies of the Jews perished; no one resisted, because they feared them. (9:2).
The governors of the satrapies, the princes, and the royal secretaries were paying honor to the Jews, because fear of Mordecai weighed upon them. (9:3).
The king’s decree required that Mordecai’s name be held in honor throughout the kingdom. (9:4).
Now in the city of Susa the Jews killed five hundred men, (9:6).
including Pharsannestain, Delphon, Phasga, (9:7).
Pharadatha, Barea, Sarbacha, (9:8).
Marmasima, Aruphaeus, Arsaeus, Zabutheus, (9:9).
the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the Bougean, the enemy of the Jews—and they indulged themselves in plunder. (9:10).
That same day, the number of those killed in Susa was reported to the king. (9:11).

The king said to Esther, “In the city of Susa, the Jews have destroyed five hundred people. What do you suppose they have done in the surrounding countryside? Whatever more you ask will be done for you.” (9:12).
And Esther said to the king, “Let the Jews be allowed to do the same tomorrow. Also, hang up the bodies of Haman’s ten sons.” (9:13).
So he permitted this to be done and handed over to the Jews of the city the bodies of Haman’s sons to hang up. (9:14).
The Jews who were in Susa gathered on the fourteenth and killed three hundred men but took no plunder. (9:15).

Now the other Jews in the kingdom gathered to defend themselves and got relief from their enemies. They destroyed fifteen thousand of them on the thirteenth of Adar but did not engage in plunder. (9:16).
On the fourteenth day of the same month they rested and kept it as a day of rest with joy and gladness. (9:17).
The Jews who were in the city of Susa came together also on the fourteenth but did not rest. They celebrated the fifteenth with joy and gladness. (9:18).

On this account, then, the Jews who are scattered around the countryside keep the fourteenth of Adar as a joyful holiday and send presents of food to one another, while those who live in the large cities keep the fifteenth day of Adar as their joyful holiday, also sending presents to one another. (9:19).
Mordecai recorded these things in a book and sent it to the Jews in the kingdom of Artaxerxes both near and far, (9:20).
to institute these days as holidays and to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar, (9:21).

for on these days the Jews got relief from their enemies. The whole month (namely, Adar) in which their condition had been changed from sorrow into gladness and from a time of distress to a holiday was to be celebrated as a time for feasting and gladness and for sending presents of food to their friends and to the poor. (9:22).
So the Jews accepted what Mordecai had written to them: (9:23).
how Haman son of Hammedatha, the Macedonian, fought against them, how he made a decree and cast lots to destroy them, (9:24).
and how he went in to the king, telling him to hang Mordecai, but the wicked plot he had devised against the Jews came back upon himself, and he and his sons were hanged. (9:25).

Therefore these days were called “Purim,” because of the lots (for in their language this is the word that means “lots”). And so, because of what was written in this letter and because of what they had experienced in this affair and what had befallen them, Mordecai established this festival, (9:26).

and the Jews took upon themselves, upon their descendants, and upon all who would join them to observe it without fail. These days of Purim should be a memorial and kept from generation to generation, in every city, family, and country. (9:27).
These days of Purim shall be observed for all time, and the commemoration of them shall never cease among their descendants. (9:28).
Then Queen Esther daughter of Aminadab along with Mordecai the Jew wrote down what they had done and gave full authority to the letter about Purim. (9:29).
And Mordecai and Queen Esther established this decision on their own responsibility, pledging their own well-being to the plan. (9:31).
Esther established it by a decree forever, and it was written for a memorial. (9:32).

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 10
summaryBullets: In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said that he was a priest and a Levite, and his son Ptolemy brought to Egypt the preceding letter about Purim, which they said was authentic and had been translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, one of the residents of Jerusalem. (10:1).
And as for his power and bravery and the wealth and glory of his kingdom, they were recorded in the annals of the kings of the Persians and the Medes. (10:2).
Mordecai succeeded King Artaxerxes and was great in the kingdom, as well as honored by the Jews. His way of life was such as to make him beloved to his whole nation. (10:3).
And Mordecai said, “These things have come from God, (10:4).
for I remember the dream that I had concerning these matters, and none of them has failed to be fulfilled. (10:5).
There was the little spring that became a river, and there was light and sun and abundant water. The river is Esther, whom the king married and made queen. (10:6).
The two dragons are Haman and myself. (10:7).
The nations are those that gathered to destroy the name of the Jews. (10:8).

And my nation, this is Israel, who cried out to God and was saved. The Lord has saved his people; the Lord has rescued us from all these evils; God has done great signs and wonders, wonders that have never happened among the nations. (10:9).
For this purpose he made two lots, one for the people of God and one for all the nations, (10:10).
and these two lots came to the hour and moment and to the day of judgment before God and among all the nations. (10:11).
And God remembered his people and vindicated his inheritance. (10:12).

So they will observe these days in the month of Adar, on the fourteenth and fifteenth of that month, with an assembly and joy and gladness before God, from generation to generation forever among his people Israel.” (10:13).
crossRefs: Genesis 41:32 — Dream confirmed by God.
Esther 6:6–11 — Mordecai honored by the king.
Psalm 126:1–3 — God restores Zion with joy.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּנִּין (tannîn, 'dragon/serpent') — Greek: δράκοντες (drákontes) — Aramaic: תניניא (tannīnyā)
translationNotes.note: Interpreted as symbolic of Mordecai and Haman, representing the conflict resolved by God’s deliverance.

stories.keyTakeaway: The narrative concludes with Mordecai exalted and his dream fulfilled, showing God’s deliverance of Israel.
